question: How do I hire a fractional CRO in Greenville?
body:
## Direct Answer
To hire a fractional CRO in Greenville, define the revenue outcome you're buying (pipeline, forecast accuracy, or a GTM rebuild), then source candidates through Upstate operator networks, fractional-executive marketplaces, and revenue-leader referrals rather than job boards. Screen for South Carolina B2B experience, agree on a 10-to-20 hour weekly cadence, and structure a 90-day scorecard before signing. Expect $8,000 to $20,000 per month depending on scope and seniority.

Hiring a fractional Chief Revenue Officer in Greenville, South Carolina is less about finding a resume and more about buying a specific revenue result on a part-time basis. The Upstate's economy — advanced manufacturing along the I-85 corridor, a growing SaaS and fintech cluster downtown, and a dense field of professional-services firms — means many companies hit $3M–$20M in revenue with a strong founder-seller but no repeatable go-to-market engine. A fractional CRO fills that gap for a fraction of a $300K+ full-time comp package. This essay walks through when the role makes sense, how to source and vet candidates locally, what to pay, and how to structure the engagement so it produces measurable lift instead of expensive advice.

## What does a fractional CRO actually do for a Greenville company?
A fractional CRO owns the entire revenue function on a part-time, contracted basis — typically one to three days a week — and is accountable for the number, not just for giving suggestions. That distinction matters more than any credential. A consultant hands you a deck and leaves; a fractional CRO sits in your pipeline reviews, rebuilds your sales process, coaches your reps, aligns marketing and customer success to a single revenue model, and reports to you (or the board) against a scorecard. For a Greenville manufacturer trying to move from relationship-based reorders to a proactive outbound motion, or a downtown SaaS startup trying to graduate from founder-led sales, that operational ownership is the whole point.

The scope usually spans four areas: go-to-market strategy (ICP, pricing, channel mix, territory design), sales execution (process, methodology, CRM hygiene, forecasting), team leadership (hiring reps, comp plans, coaching cadence), and cross-functional alignment (marketing pipeline handoff, customer success expansion). A good fractional CRO diagnoses which of these is actually broken before touching anything else. Many Upstate companies believe they have a "we need more leads" problem when they actually have a conversion or forecasting problem — the CRO's first job is to tell you which one is true. For a deeper breakdown of the role boundary, see the PULSE explainer on the [fractional revenue leader operating model](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10241).

Crucially, a fractional CRO is not a fractional VP of Sales. The CRO title implies ownership of *all* revenue — new sales, expansion, retention, and often marketing — whereas a VP of Sales owns the closing motion alone. Buy the title that matches your gap. If your churn is fine and marketing is solid but your closers are inconsistent, a fractional sales leader is cheaper and more precise. If revenue is leaking across the whole funnel, the CRO scope is justified.

## When is the right time for a Greenville company to hire one?
The clearest trigger is a revenue plateau with a founder who has become the bottleneck. In the Upstate, an enormous number of companies grow to $2M–$8M on the founder's personal network and reputation — think a Greenville industrial-services firm whose owner closes every major account by relationship. That model has a ceiling. When the founder can no longer personally touch every deal and the next tier of salespeople isn't producing, revenue flattens. That's the moment a fractional CRO earns their fee: they build the system that lets revenue grow without the founder in every room.

Other strong signals include a recent capital raise or acquisition that demands a step-change in growth, an unpredictable forecast (you genuinely don't know if you'll hit the quarter until the last week), a sales team that's grown past three or four reps with no formal process, or a pending full-time CRO hire you're not ready to commit $300K+ to. Fractional lets you install senior leadership now and convert to full-time later if the scale justifies it. Many Greenville companies use the fractional engagement explicitly as a "try before you buy" bridge.

The wrong time is equally important to name. If you have no product-market fit, a CRO can't manufacture demand that the market isn't signaling — you need founders in customer conversations, not an org chart. If you can't afford at least a six-month runway at the engagement rate, you'll cut the relationship before the system compounds; revenue systems take two to three quarters to show durable lift. And if leadership won't cede real authority over the sales process, the CRO becomes an expensive advisor whose recommendations die in committee. Honest readiness is a prerequisite. The PULSE guide to [revenue-leadership readiness signals](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10488) covers the go/no-go checklist in detail.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Revenue plateau or founder bottleneck] --> B{Is there product market fit}
  B -->|No| C[Fix PMF first not a CRO problem]
  B -->|Yes| D{Can you fund six months}
  D -->|No| E[Wait or reduce scope]
  D -->|Yes| F{Will leadership cede sales authority}
  F -->|No| G[Coaching engagement only]
  F -->|Yes| H[Hire fractional CRO]
```

## Where do I actually find fractional CRO candidates in Greenville?
Job boards are the weakest channel for this role because the best fractional executives are never actively looking — they're referred. Start with the Upstate's operator network. Greenville has an unusually tight community of revenue leaders who have scaled companies here, and warm introductions travel fast. Tap the NEXT Innovation Center and VentureSouth (the local angel network) for portfolio-company revenue leaders, the Greenville Chamber's professional groups, and the Upstate chapters of national sales communities like Pavilion and the RevOps Co-op. A single well-placed ask in these circles usually surfaces two or three credible names.

Second, use fractional-executive marketplaces that vet for seniority: Chief Outsiders, Bolster, Go Fractional, Continuum, and Pavilion's talent network all list fractional CROs, many of whom work remotely with clients nationwide. Don't over-index on "must live in Greenville" — the best fractional CRO for your business may be a former SaaS revenue leader in Charlotte or Atlanta who spends one day a week on-site. Geography matters far less than industry fit and availability. That said, a leader with genuine Upstate and Carolinas B2B experience understands the local buyer, the manufacturing sales cycle, and the talent pool you'll recruit reps from — a real advantage for territory and hiring decisions.

Third, mine your own network's exits. Ask peer founders, your fractional CFO (if you have one — they often know the whole fractional-executive bench), your board, and your investors who they've watched turn around a revenue function. Referrals from people who have *seen the candidate operate* are worth ten cold profiles. When you evaluate the funnel of candidates, treat it like any other pipeline: source wide, qualify hard, and reference-check the finalists relentlessly. The PULSE playbook on [sourcing fractional executives](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10592) maps each of these channels to the profile they tend to produce.

## How do I vet a fractional CRO so I don't buy expensive advice?
Vetting a fractional CRO is fundamentally a test of operational specificity. Anyone can talk about "building a repeatable go-to-market motion" in the abstract. The candidate you want can tell you exactly what they'd do in your business in the first 30, 60, and 90 days — and the answer changes based on your industry, deal size, and current gaps. Vague strategic language is the single biggest red flag. Push every claim toward a concrete number: "What was the pipeline coverage ratio before and after you fixed it?" "What did win rate do?" "How long did it take?"

Structure your evaluation around evidence, not charisma. Ask for two or three specific turnarounds where they owned the number, and get the metrics: revenue growth, forecast accuracy improvement, sales-cycle compression, quota attainment across the team. Then reference-check those stories directly with the CEO or founder they worked under — not the references they hand you, but people you find on your own who overlapped with them. Confirm industry adjacency: a CRO who scaled transactional SaaS may struggle with a Greenville manufacturer's nine-month, multi-stakeholder capital-equipment sale, and vice versa. Motion fit matters as much as seniority.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Candidate pool] --> B[Screen for owned the number not advised]
  B --> C[Verify industry and deal motion fit]
  C --> D[Reference check founders they reported to]
  D --> E[Paid diagnostic sprint two to four weeks]
  E --> F[Ninety day scorecard agreed]
  F --> G[Full engagement]
```

The highest-signal vetting move is a paid diagnostic sprint before any long-term commitment. Pay the candidate for two to four weeks to audit your revenue function and deliver a prioritized plan. You learn three things at once: how they think, how they operate inside your actual data, and whether your teams respond to them. A great fractional CRO will surface problems you didn't know you had; a mediocre one will regurgitate generic frameworks. This small paid trial de-risks the entire relationship far better than another interview round. Pair it with the diagnostic questions in the PULSE guide to [evaluating revenue-leader candidates](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10715).

## What should I expect to pay, and how do I structure the deal?
Fractional CRO pricing in the Greenville market generally runs $8,000 to $20,000 per month, driven by the candidate's seniority, the weekly time commitment, and scope. A one-day-a-week engagement with a strong operator lands near the lower end; a two-to-three-day engagement with someone who has scaled multiple companies to exit sits toward the top. This is dramatically cheaper than a full-time CRO, whose base plus bonus plus equity in the Carolinas commonly exceeds $250,000–$350,000 all-in. The fractional model exists precisely because a $10M-revenue company needs CRO-level judgment but not CRO-level hours.

Three structures dominate. A flat monthly retainer for a defined day-per-week cadence is the most common and the easiest to budget. Project-based pricing works when the mandate is bounded — "rebuild the comp plan and stand up an outbound team in one quarter." And a base-plus-incentive structure ties part of the fee to revenue outcomes, which aligns interests but requires clean attribution and mutual trust; it works best after you've established a track record together, not on day one. Whatever the shape, insist on a defined scope, a fixed weekly time commitment in writing, and a 90-day scorecard with two or three metrics you'll both watch — pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, and win rate are the usual suspects.

Protect yourself on the exit and the intangibles. Use a 30-day mutual termination clause so either side can walk if the fit is wrong. Confirm the candidate's other client load — a fractional CRO juggling six clients can't give yours real attention; three to four is a healthier ceiling. Get clarity on whether they'll be genuinely present for your team (Slack, pipeline reviews, deal desk) or just a monthly strategy call. And write down what "success" means before the first invoice, so the 90-day review is a scoreboard, not an argument. The PULSE breakdown of [fractional executive engagement terms](https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/q10883) includes a sample scope-of-work you can adapt.

## How do I onboard a fractional CRO so the first 90 days actually produce lift?
The engagement lives or dies in the first two weeks. Give the fractional CRO fast, complete access — CRM, pipeline data, win/loss history, comp plans, marketing metrics, and unfiltered time with your reps and customers. Withholding data to "protect" the team only delays the diagnosis you're paying for. The best first move is a listening tour: the CRO interviews every rep, sits in on live deals, and talks to a handful of recent won and lost accounts. In a Greenville context, that often means riding along on in-person visits to Upstate accounts, because a lot of the real sales intelligence never makes it into the CRM.

Then insist on a written 30/60/90 plan with a small number of prioritized bets rather than a boil-the-ocean transformation. A disciplined fractional CRO fixes the highest-leverage constraint first — usually forecasting discipline or pipeline hygiene — and shows a visible win inside the first month to build credibility with a skeptical sales team. Internal buy-in is the silent failure mode: a brilliant plan the reps resist will underperform a good plan the reps own. Have the CRO co-author the changes with your existing leaders, and back their authority publicly so the org knows this isn't optional. Review progress against the scorecard every two weeks, not once at day 90 — early course-correction is the entire advantage of the fractional model over a big-bang consulting project.

## Related questions
### What's the difference between a fractional CRO and a sales consultant?
A fractional CRO owns the revenue number and operates inside your team — hiring, forecasting, coaching — while a consultant advises and hands off a plan. Buy a CRO for accountability, a consultant for a one-time diagnosis.

### Can a fractional CRO work fully remote for a Greenville company?
Yes. Most fractional CROs blend remote work with periodic on-site days. For Upstate manufacturers with in-person, relationship-driven sales, negotiate at least monthly on-site presence for ride-alongs and team coaching.

### How long should a fractional CRO engagement last?
Typically six to eighteen months. It takes two to three quarters for revenue-system changes to compound, and many engagements either convert to full-time or taper to a lighter advisory cadence once the machine runs itself.

### Is a fractional CRO worth it for a company under $2M in revenue?
Usually not at full CRO scope. Below $2M, a fractional VP of Sales or a lighter advisory engagement is more cost-appropriate; full CRO ownership pays off once you have multiple reps and cross-functional revenue complexity.

### How do I measure whether the fractional CRO is working?
Track three to five metrics against a 90-day baseline: pipeline coverage ratio, forecast accuracy, win rate, sales-cycle length, and quota attainment. Agree on these before signing so the review is objective.

## FAQ
**How much does a fractional CRO cost in Greenville, SC?**
Generally $8,000 to $20,000 per month depending on seniority, weekly hours, and scope — far below a full-time CRO's $250K–$350K all-in Carolinas comp. One day a week sits near the low end; two to three days with a proven multi-exit operator sits near the top.

**How many hours a week does a fractional CRO work?**
Most engagements run one to three days per week (roughly 8–24 hours). The right number depends on how much active rebuilding is happening — heavier at the start during the diagnostic and system build, often tapering once processes stabilize.

**Should the fractional CRO have specific South Carolina or manufacturing experience?**
Industry and sales-motion fit matter more than a Greenville zip code, but a leader with Carolinas B2B or Upstate manufacturing experience understands the local buyer, the longer capital-equipment sales cycle, and the regional talent pool you'll recruit reps from — a genuine edge for territory and hiring decisions.

**Can I convert a fractional CRO to a full-time hire?**
Often, yes, and many companies use fractional explicitly as a try-before-you-buy path. Clarify conversion terms up front — whether the fractional fees credit against a future package, and whether the candidate even wants a full-time seat, since many career fractional executives do not.

**What's the biggest mistake companies make hiring a fractional CRO?**
Hiring one before product-market fit, or refusing to give them real authority over the sales process. Both turn an operator into an expensive advisor. The second biggest mistake is skipping the reference checks and paid diagnostic that separate operators from talkers.

**How do I know if I need a fractional CRO versus a fractional VP of Sales?**
If revenue leaks across the whole funnel — new sales, marketing handoff, and retention — you need the CRO's broader ownership. If only the closing motion is inconsistent while marketing and churn are healthy, a fractional VP of Sales is cheaper and more precise.

**How fast should I expect results?**
Expect a visible early win — cleaner pipeline, a tighter forecast, a fixed comp plan — inside the first 30–45 days, but durable revenue lift over two to three quarters. Anyone promising a hockey-stick in 30 days is selling, not operating.

**What should be in the contract?**
A defined scope of work, a fixed weekly time commitment, a 90-day scorecard with two or three agreed metrics, a 30-day mutual termination clause, clarity on other client load, and IP/confidentiality terms. Put "what success means" in writing before the first invoice.
